newsitem.title: BULGARIA: Bulgaria's UDF seeks all-party support to end crisis.
newsitem.headline: Bulgaria's UDF seeks all-party support to end crisis.

text.p: The Union of Democratic Forces, which won a big parliamentary majority in Saturday's elections, said it would meet other parties on Tuesday to seek their support for its programme to lead Bulgaria out of crisis.

UDF leader Ivan Kostov said on Monday his priorities were carrying out reforms agreed with the International Monetary Fund, fighting organised crime and corruption, opening secret police files on public figures and bringing Bulgaria into the European Union and NATO.

"We are proposing that the newly formed parliament pass an anti-crisis declaration, and tomorrow we start talks with the other main forces for agreement on its principles," Kostov told a news conference.

With all but a handful of results counted, the electoral commission said the UDF had 137 seats in the 240-seat assembly to the former ruling Socialists' 57. Three smaller parties will also enter parliament.
Kostov said he hoped the agreement would include the Socialists.

"I think dialogue with the Socialist Party is possible, after all its current leadership helped resolve the January crisis and signed the declaration for support for the actions of the caretaker government," he said.

Asked about a formal coalition, he said various options would be considered. "Anyway, I am optimistic that in the course of the talks we shall find the formula of the agreement in the name of the country's future," he said.
The UDF's ruling National Executive Bureau meets on Thursday and is expected to nominate Kostov as prime minister and decide on the make-up of the future UDF cabinet.
Deputy Prime Minister Alexander Bozhkov is expected to retain the trade portfolio, overseeing the restructuring of the state sector.

Economic Policy Minister Krassimir Angarski is expected to take the finance portfolio, and Bogomil Bonev is expected to continue his campaign against organised crime and corruption at the interior ministry.

The first task of the new parliament will be to pass a 1997 budget and package of banking laws needed to implement a currency board, a restrictive fixed exchange rate regime agreed with the IMF as a condition for a $657 million funding deal.

Privatising and restructuring the state sector, freeing prices and trade rules and providing an investor-friendly legal climate to aid a swift transition to a market economy are also crucial steps which the new government must take.

Bulgarian Brady bonds rose sharply on the secondary debt market on the news of the UDF victory. An outlook report from Banque Nationale de Paris said the bonds could outperform the global Brady index under a currency board.
The combination of falling inflation with a strengthening currency underpinned by fiscal adjustment and wide-scale undustrial restructuring was ideal for bond investors, the report said.
The lev traded lower on the interbank market on Monday, but Finance Minister Svetoslav Gavriiski blamed speculation, saying traders were buying dollars in anticipation of a lev fall.
